content_metadata.description: This video provides an informative overview of active galaxies and quasars, focusing on their characteristics, types, and energy sources.

qAndA.answer: Active galaxies are more luminous, and they emit non-stellar radiation, which is not produced by the thermal activity of stars.
qAndA.question: What are the two primary differences between normal galaxies and active galaxies?
What type of active galaxy is often characterized by powerful jets of material streaming outward?

qAndA.answer: Their spectral lines didn't match with any known elements on Earth.
qAndA.question: What was the initial puzzle about quasars that made them mysterious?

qAndA.answer: They appeared star-like in images due to their immense distances.
qAndA.question: Why did astronomers initially think quasars were stars?

qAndA.answer: By observing the speed at which the quasar's brightness varies. The faster the variation, the smaller the energy source must be.
qAndA.question: How do astronomers determine the size of a quasar's energy source?

narrativeProgression.description: The video title and topic are introduced.
The lecturer welcomes the audience and outlines the lecture's focus on active galaxies and quasars.
The lecturer defines active galaxies, highlighting their increased luminosity and emission of non-stellar radiation.
The lecturer discusses different types of active galaxies: Seyfert galaxies, radio galaxies, and blazars.
The lecturer focuses on radio galaxies, describing their excess radio emission and common feature of material jets.

props.name: Image of a radio galaxy with prominent jets

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer describes blazars as compact centers of elliptical galaxies with a high energy output.
The lecturer transitions to quasars, explaining their star-like appearance, radio wave emission, and initially puzzling spectral lines.

props.name: Slide with bullet points about quasars

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer reveals that quasars are not stars but the extremely bright nuclei of distant galaxies.

props.name: Slide with bullet points about the nature of quasars

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer reinforces the relationship between Hubble's Law and quasars, emphasizing their vast distances and ancient origins.

props.name: Slide with bullet points about Hubble's Law and quasars
Two images showing a quasar and the faint surrounding galaxy after masking

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer explains that the rapid brightness variation of quasars implies a compact energy source, smaller than a solar system.

props.name: Slide with bullet points explaining the constraint on the size of the quasar's energy source
Diagram illustrating light travel time limits brightness variation

scenes.title: Size of the Energy Source: Brightness Variation

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer concludes that the immense energy output from a small region must be powered by supermassive black holes accreting matter.

props.name: Slide with bullet points identifying supermassive black holes as the energy source for quasars
Image of a supermassive black hole with an accretion disk

scenes.title: Energy Source of Quasars: Supermassive Black Holes

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer summarizes the key differences between active and normal galaxies, the nature of quasars, and the role of supermassive black holes as their energy source.

activities.description: The slide changes to a plain background with the word 'License'.

narrativeProgression.description: The lecture concludes, and licensing information is displayed.

climax.description: The climax occurs when the supermassive black hole is revealed as the energy source for quasars.

youtube_description:
In this lecture, we will look at active galaxies and their properties and types. In addition, we will look a bit closer at a specific type of active galaxy known as a quasar.

These lecture videos are designed to complement the content in the OpenStax Astronomy 2e textbook. The book can be downloaded free of charge at: https://openstax.org/details/books/astronomy-2e

I can be reached with comments at wagnerastronomy@gmail.com. However, classes I am teaching receive priority so I will try to respond as I can to questions.

Note: Lesson 0 materials are specific for the classes that I teach. Lesson 1 will start with Chapter 1 of the textbook.

You can access the most current versions through the following playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMahwAGxKuWlWcYdu2hPMmcD_pyQWkZ7J

These videos have been updated for 2023 and are being released under a CC-BY license so that others can feel free to adapt them for their use as long as attribution is given. 

Lecture slides are available for download here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12JnRLzV-o4xl5KnJ39bGyK27qG7s0Lnw?usp=sharing They are currently available only in Apple Keynote format. As each chapter is recorded and I have verified that the slides are correct, I will load PowerPoint and pdf versions through the same link above.
